question: Two weeks ago, German farmers took to the streets to protest against the measures taken by the German government. At the start of this week, it was the turn of French farmers to raise their voices. Today, Polish farmers are joining the movement.

Their anger is directed against national governments, but we know perfectly well that their policies only follow EU legislation, which leaves governments little or no room for manoeuvre, particularly as regards the CAP and the integration of the Ukrainian market. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission intend to impose the same obligations concerning plant protection products for farmers in third countries as for those in EU countries?
How can it integrate the Ukrainian market without deregulating the European agricultural market?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.4.2024) Regulation (EC) No 1107/20091 deals with the placing of plant protection products on the market, ensuring a high level of protection of both human and animal health and the environment while safeguarding the competitiveness of EU agriculture. The jurisdiction of this Regulation is limited to the EU and is not applicable to third countries.
However, all food and feed, produced in the EU or imported from third countries, when placed on the EU market must comply with the maximum residue levels (MRLs) set in Regulation (EC) No 396/20052.

Since 4 June 2022, the EU has fully liberalised all imports from Ukraine under Autonomous Trade Measures (ATMs3) that, together with the Solidarity Lanes4, contribute towards keeping trade flows from Ukraine to the EU and to the rest of the world at a stable level despite the disruptions caused by Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.

While the monitoring of imports of agricultural goods from Ukraine showed an increased influx of agricultural products notably in Member States bordering Ukraine, it has not shown adverse effects on the EU market as a whole.

Aware that adverse effects may be more localised, the Commission has therefore included in its proposal5 to extend the current ATMs beyond 5 June 2024, a strengthened safeguard mechanism that also takes into account the impact in one or more Member States, and an automatic safeguard for eggs, poultry and sugar - which Council and Parliament have extended to honey, maize, oats and groats- to protect EU producers6.
The Commission considers that the new ATM Regulation will continue to ensure that imports of Ukrainian agricultural products do not destabilise the EU agricultural market.
